title: Not my worth
carry: what was lost was held, not who you are

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dishes and the fevers and the langar: work nobody pays for. Your line was I saw what you did, and it mattered. Whom did you thank? Today, what's left of a person when the work is gone. Day nine hundred thirteen.
screen: `I SAW WHAT YOU DID, AND IT MATTERED.`

segments.voice: The badge stops working at the door. Or the email arrives with a meeting invitation from someone in human resources. Or the shop that was going to last forever puts a sign in the window. Or the body says no more to the job it did for years. However it comes, losing work can feel like losing a name. At a party, someone asks, so what do you do? And for a while there's no easy answer. Today: Epictetus.
screen: `THE BADGE STOPS WORKING.` → `SO WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO EASY ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the confusion. A job gives us a schedule, colleagues, a title, a paycheck, and a ready answer at parties. It's easy to fuse all of that into a sense of who we are. Then, when the job goes, it can seem as if we've gone with it. Second, a Stoic teacher. Epictetus taught philosophy in the Roman world. His handbook opens with a sorting of the world: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Among the things he says are not in our power: our body, our property, our reputation, our offices, the positions we hold. What is in our power is how we judge, what we aim for, what we turn away from. For Epictetus, a person's worth lives on that inside list. A job is on the outside list. It can be given and taken. In his view, it was never the measure of a person. Third, a man who lost everything. In the book of Job, in the Hebrew Bible, Job loses his wealth, his household, his children, all in one day. And he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Later in the book he argues, mourns and protests at length, and the text lets him. Some readers hear a distinction in that first line: what was given can be taken, and the one it was given to is still there. Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a claim that losing work doesn't hurt, or doesn't matter. Rent matters. Purpose matters. Grief is fair, and Job is given room for it. Epictetus, for his part, would ask for a cooler sorting. What the two share is a narrower line: what was lost was held, not who you are, and the person who held it is still there.
screen: `A JOB FUSED WITH A SELF.` · `IN OUR POWER, AND NOT.` · `THE LORD GAVE, AND HATH TAKEN.` · `IT HURTS, AND IT'S NOT YOUR WORTH.` · then, large: `NOT MY WORTH.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, sort the way Epictetus did. Breathe slowly. Picture two baskets. In the outer basket, place the things that can be given and taken: a title, a desk, a salary, how others see you. Set them in gently, one at a time. Now notice what's left in you, as you sit here breathing: the way you pay attention, what you care about, how you choose to meet this day. That's the inner basket. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus. The Stoic teacher who sorted the world into what's in our power and what isn't, and put a job on the outside list. Today's word.

Your line: what was lost was held, not who you are. Today, when someone asks what you do, or when you ask yourself, add one thing about who you are that has nothing to do with a job. Day nine hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: People facing job loss often lean on community, faith or philosophy to keep their sense of worth apart from their work; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's sorting of what is and isn't in our power, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job.

myth: for Epictetus, the positions we hold are in our power
he lists offices with body, property and reputation among the things not in our power.
the book of Job lets Job argue, mourn and protest after his losses
the text gives his protest room; the first line is not the whole story.
saying a job isn't your worth means losing it shouldn't hurt
rent, purpose and grief are real; the claim is only that worth wasn't what was lost.

fork.setup: you're Epictetus, sorting the world into what's in our power and what isn't. where does a person's job title go?
fork.reveal: he lists offices, the positions we hold, with body, property and reputation: not in our power. what is in our power is how we judge and what we aim for.

trapdoor: what you thought: losing a job means losing part of yourself.
what it means: work can be given and taken, and losing it hurts, but your worth isn't what went.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus's opening sorting in the Enchiridion, with offices on the not-in-our-power side, and Job's line that what was given can be taken from one who remains.

notes: Epictetus's biography (born a slave) is left out under the claims rule.

Check Long's list in Enchiridion 1 (body, property, reputation, offices/magisterial power) and the inside list (opinion, movement toward a thing, desire, aversion), here paraphrased as how we judge, what we aim for, what we turn away from.
Job 1:13–19 has the losses come in one series of messages; 'all in one day' follows verse 13. Children are named among the losses; check tone.
The script avoids financial or career advice and does not tell the listener what they feel.
Editor: removed 'the second question is often' (frequency claim); ending reframed as the texts' claim rather than the narrator telling the listener what is true of them.

Audit (serious): the teach said both Epictetus and Job claim that what was lost 'can be named and grieved'; Epictetus counsels against being disturbed by the loss of externals, so grief is now attributed only to Job's book, and the Job 1:21 'distinction' is marked as a reading ('some readers hear'), not the verse's plain sense.
